messages.subject: Drawing from a posterior distribution
parts:
Dear All,
I've gotten myself quite stuck trying to implement what seems like it should be a straightforward linear mixed-effects model in rstan. The objective is to predict the growth rates of 281 species of trees from their functional traits. There is substantial variation in growth rates among the 24 geographical sites, which is why i include the 'random effects' terms. The model converges well and gives sensible results. I've used the matt trick, which sped up convergence dramatically. 

The problem begins when I attempt to incorporate measurement error in growth rates. As long as I use only point estimates of the growth rates for each species (species-mean growth rates), all is fine. But I would like to include within-species uncertainty in growth. One way to do this is to use the point estimates of growth for every individual within every species. But since the number of individuals per species varies widely (5-2205, median 39), I fear this would result in a few species dominating the analysis.

Thus, it would be nice to be able to draw a random deviate for each species from species-specific log normal distributions at every iteration through the model. I have posterior estimates of growth rates for each species from an previous set of models. There is a function to draw lognormal deviates, but it only works in the generated quantities block, which is of little use in my situation. Would it be possible to modify the lognormal_rng() command to allow it to be used in the model block?

Another solution would be to run an individual-level analysis, using only up to 50 (or so) individuals per species. But this seems a bit wasteful. I would like to be able to use all of my data.

An additional question: I am running this model to look at the variation in the growth rate-functional trait relationship among members of three different groups: taxonomic families (48), continents (6), and between temperate and tropical zones (2). Is it correct to include hyperparameters in all three versions of the model?

Any comments or suggestions would be much appreciated.
cordially,
tim paine

 The following model fails to compile, owing to the lognormal_rng() command in the model block.
// this model the SGR-trt relationship for each continent and global
data{
    int <lower=0> n_spp       ; // indicates number of species  // 281
    int <lower=0> n_group     ; // indicates number of groups 48, 6, or 2
    int <lower=0> n_site      ; // indicates number of sites //24

    int <lower=1> group[n_spp]; // the group membership of each species
    int <lower=1> site [n_spp]; // the site of each species

    vector [n_spp] obsSGR_m   ; // mean SGR observed for each species
    vector<lower=0>[n_spp] obsSGR_sd; // SD of SGR observed for each species. bounded at 0 bc it's a SD
    vector [n_spp] sla_m      ; // vector of mean SLA, one per species
    }

parameters{
     vector [n_site]          inter_raw  ;    // set of intercepts to define SGR at global mean trts (trts centered & standardized!), one per group
     vector [n_site]          site_sla_slope_raw; // set of slopes for site effect of SLA on SGR (trts centered & standardized!), one per site
     vector [n_group]         slope_sla_raw ; // set of slopes to define SGR at global mean SLA (trts centered & standardized!), one per group
     real <lower=0, upper=10> sigma_SGR;      // single sigma for growth rate for all levels
 
  // hyperparams //
     real <lower=0, upper=10> site_sla_sd   ; // standard deviation - must be positive
     real                     inter_mean    ; // an overall intercept
     real <lower=0, upper=10> inter_sd      ; // standard deviation - must be positive
     real                     slope_sla_mean; // overall mean wd-SGR slope
     real <lower=0, upper=10> slope_sla_sd  ; // standard deviation - must be positive
     }
   
transformed parameters{
    vector [n_site ]  inter;  
    vector [n_site ]  site_sla_slope;  
    vector [n_group]  slope_sla;  
    inter         <-                  inter_sd     * inter_raw;
    site_sla_slope<-                  site_sla_sd  * site_sla_slope_raw;
    slope_sla     <- slope_sla_mean + slope_sla_sd * slope_sla_raw;
    }

model{
    vector [n_spp] predSGR;         // and for those predicted from trait values

    // diffuse priors on hyperparameters
        inter_mean     ~ normal(0,10);
        inter_sd       ~ cauchy(0,10);
        slope_sla_mean ~ normal(0,10);
        slope_sla_sd   ~ cauchy(0,10);
        site_sla_sd    ~ cauchy(0,10);

    // these imply: beta ~ normal(mu_beta,sigma_beta)
    inter_raw          ~ normal(0, 1);
    site_sla_slope_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
    slope_sla_raw      ~ normal(0, 1);

    // in each iteration, draw a log-normal variate for each species, given its mean and sd of SGR. obsSGR_m is already log-transformed in R
    vector [n_spp] obsSGR_w_error;
    obsSGR_w_error <- lognormal_rng(obsSGR_m, obsSGR_sd);

    // Prepare the observed SGR and predicted SGRs for analysis
    for(i in 1:n_spp){
         predSGR[i] <- inter[site[i]] + inter_mean + (site_sla_slope[site[i]] + slope_sla[group[i]])*sla_m[i];
         }
     obsSGR_w_error ~ normal(predSGR, sigma_SGR);
  }

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Drawing from a posterior distribution
parts:
Hi Tim,

I am guessing you are thinking in terms of a Gibbs sampler, which while Bayesian is not Stanian. Stan evaluates the joint posterior and decides to accept proposals with a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance step where the proposal is generated in a somewhat complicated fashion using Hamiltonians. So, it doesn't make sense to draw a random proposal for a parameter inside the model block of a .stan file. I think the proposals in Stan are actually deterministic once you condition on the realization of the momentum, although there is randomness in whether the proposal is accepted.

In any event, it sounds like what you are trying to do would be to put a log-normal prior on the species-specific parameters where the location and scale of this log-normal distribution are fixed or perhaps are unknown parameters with informative priors. If so, you can just do that in the model block.

The generated quantities block is for auxiliary calculations that are not part of the model and in that case, drawing randomly from a posterior predictive distribution can be a reasonable thing to do.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Drawing from a posterior distribution
parts:
On 6/17/13 12:29 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> ... I think the proposals in Stan are actually deterministic once you
> condition on the realization of the momentum, although there is randomness in whether the proposal is accepted.

That's true in basic HMC, but not NUTS. In NUTS, there's a randomization for
the direction to extend the subtree (forward or backward in time). Nobody's
figured out how to maintain detailed balance without that randomization.

- Bob

Essentially, I am trying to acknowledege that SGR is estimated with error, and I have a quantification of that uncertainty (obsSGR_sd). Given that I am providing a fixed (data-defined) prior, I don't see how I could specify initial values that would help.

Additionally, is there an example that demonstrates the use of fixed priors? I have not been able to locate one.

Thank you for being patient with my obtuseness.
best wishes,

On Monday, June 17, 2013 5:29:22 AM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:
Hi Tim,

I am guessing you are thinking in terms of a Gibbs sampler, which while Bayesian is not Stanian. Stan evaluates the joint posterior and decides to accept proposals with a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance step where the proposal is generated in a somewhat complicated fashion using Hamiltonians. So, it doesn't make sense to draw a random proposal for a parameter inside the model block of a .stan file. I think the proposals in Stan are actually deterministic once you condition on the realization of the momentum, although there is randomness in whether the proposal is accepted.

In any event, it sounds like what you are trying to do would be to put a log-normal prior on the species-specific parameters where the location and scale of this log-normal distribution are fixed or perhaps are unknown parameters with informative priors. If so, you can just do that in the model block.

The generated quantities block is for auxiliary calculations that are not part of the model and in that case, drawing randomly from a posterior predictive distribution can be a reasonable thing to do.

Ben

On Sunday, June 16, 2013 11:33:02 PM UTC-4, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
I am not sure what you are trying to do.  But it seems to me you are not dong Bayesian.  Simply speaking, Stan allows to specify the posterior distribution and do sampling.  And everything else is based on this.  If you can represent your problem with a Bayesian model, it would be fine.  

Jiqiang

parts:
On 6/18/13 5:31 AM, cetp wrote:
> Dear Ben et al,
> Thank you for your quick and informative responses. You are right that I was thinking of the Gibbs sampler, rather than
> understanding the Stanian approach, the details of which remain beyond me. You are also right that what I am trying to
> do is to put a lognormal prior on SGR. I was using confused terminology before.
>
> The problem is that SGR is my response variable, rather than a predictor. Essentially, I am trying to acknowledege that
> SGR is estimated with error, and I have a quantification of that uncertainty (obsSGR_sd). I have modified the model to
> include a fixed lognormal prior on obsSGR (please see attached code). The model compiles, but fails to initialize with
> the error "Initialization failed after 100 attempts. Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained
> values, or reparameterizing the model." Given that I am providing a fixed (data-defined) prior, I don't see how I could
> specify initial values that would help.
>
> Additionally, is there an example that demonstrates the use of fixed priors? I have not been able to locate one.

1. There's a chapter that includes a section on measurement
error in the model and there's an entire chapter of Andrew's
Baysesian Data Analysis book on measurement error with many
more examples.

2. As always, I'd recommend that you start with a simpler model
and work up to what you're trying to do. For instance, define
the model without measurement error, then add a measurement
error component. The purpose is to isolate where the problems
are one step at a time, because it's hard to debug a complex
model.

3. There are (at least) two problems with the model you specified,
the relevant bits of which are:

data{
...

vector [n_spp] obsSGR_m ; // mean SGR estimated for each species. already log-transformed (in R)
vector<lower=0> [n_spp] obsSGR_sd ; // SD of SGR estimated for each species. bounded at 0 bc it's a SD

}
model {
vector [n_spp] predSGR; // predicted from trait values

....
obsSGR_w_error <- lognormal_rng(obsSGR_m, obsSGR_sd);
...
obsSGR_w_error ~ normal(predSGR, sigma_SGR);
...
}

Problem number one is that the _rng functions aren't available
in the model block --- only in generated quantities. So you
need to define the "true" measurement as a parameter with appropriate
constraints.

I'm also confused about the intent of your model. It looks
like you're using lognormal measurement error In a typical
measurement error model, you'd have something like this:

data {
... meas_with_error;
... meas_noise;
...
}
parameters {
... true_meas;
...
}
model {

meas_with_error ~ foo(true_meas, meas_noise);

true_meas ~ bar(...);

}

This draws the observation meas_with_error from an
unknonw true_meas, and then uses the true_meas as if it
were data.

You put the errorful measurement on the left side twice, which
muddies the water a bit conceptually. In Stan, putting the
same value on the left side of a sampling statement twice is
the same thing as giving it the product of the densities.

On the other hand, if foo() is the normal distribution, it can
be equivalent because

a ~ normal(b,c)

has the same log probability as:

b ~ normal(a,c).

And all Stan cares about is getting the log probability right.

- Bob
